recommendations.section: 2.2 Key Comorbidities; 3.2 Treatment Decision; Decision Table 1
recommendations.title: Lower Pharmacotherapy Threshold with Diabetes or CKD
recommendations.content:
Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus. Patients with diabetes face accelerated vascular damage from hypertension. Current evidence supports a lower treatment threshold (systolic blood pressure (SBP) >= 130 mmHg) and more aggressive follow-up intervals in this population. Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors such as lisinopril are preferred as first-line agents due to their renal protective effects.

Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD). Patients with Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) are at elevated risk for both cardiovascular events and progression of renal disease. As with diabetes, a lower treatment threshold is recommended. Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors are preferred for their demonstrated renal protective benefits. More frequent laboratory monitoring is necessary to detect early changes in renal function.

## 3.2 Treatment Decision

The decision to initiate pharmacological therapy versus lifestyle modification alone is based on the patient's systolic blood pressure and the presence of comorbid conditions that increase cardiovascular risk.

## Decision Table 1: Treatment Recommendation

The following table defines the recommended initial treatment action based on systolic blood pressure and comorbidity status:

| Systolic Blood Pressure (BP) (mmHg) | Has Diabetes | Has Kidney Disease | Action | Medication | Dose | Follow-up (weeks) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| >= 140 | No | No | Start medication | Lisinopril | 10 mg daily | 4 |
| >= 130 | Yes | No | Start medication | Lisinopril | 10 mg daily | 2 |
| >= 130 | No | Yes | Start medication | Lisinopril | 10 mg daily | 2 |
| >= 130 | Yes | Yes | Start medication | Lisinopril | 10 mg daily | 2 |
| 130-139 | No | No | Lifestyle modification only | - | - | 8 |
| < 130 | No | No | Lifestyle modification only | - | - | 12 |
| < 130 | Yes | No | Lifestyle modification only | - | - | 12 |
| < 130 | No | Yes | Lifestyle modification only | - | - | 12 |

## Key principles:

- 1 Patients with Stage 2 hypertension (systolic blood pressure (SBP) >= 140) should begin pharmacological therapy regardless of comorbidity status.
- 1 Patients with Stage 1 hypertension (systolic blood pressure (SBP) 130-139) AND diabetes or chronic kidney disease should begin pharmacological therapy due to elevated cardiovascular risk.
- 1 Patients with Stage 1 hypertension without high-risk comorbidities should attempt lifestyle modification for 8 weeks before reassessment.
- 1 Patients with elevated but sub-hypertensive blood pressure (systolic blood pressure (SBP) < 130) should focus on lifestyle modifications with follow-up in 12 weeks.

Lisinopril (an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor) is recommended as the first-line agent due to its well-established efficacy, renal protective effects, and favorable side effect profile.

recommendations.title: DASH Diet and Sodium Restriction and Other Lifestyle Modification Counseling
recommendations.content:
All patients with hypertension, regardless of whether pharmacological therapy is initiated, should receive counseling on the following lifestyle modifications:

- 1 Dietary changes: Adopt the Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension (DASH) diet, which emphasizes fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and low-fat dairy products while limiting saturated fat and sodium intake to less than 2,300 mg per day.
- 1 Physical activity: Engage in at least 150 minutes per week of moderate-intensity aerobic exercise, such as brisk walking, or 75 minutes per week of vigorous-intensity aerobic exercise.
- 1 Weight management: Achieve and maintain a healthy body weight (Body Mass Index (BMI) 18.5-24.9 kg/m2). Even modest weight loss of 5-10% can significantly reduce blood pressure.
- 1 Alcohol limitation: Limit alcohol intake to no more than 2 drinks per day for men and 1 drink per day for women.
- 1 Smoking cessation: If applicable, provide smoking cessation counseling and resources.

recommendations.title: Structured Home Blood Pressure Measurement and Weekly Review
recommendations.content: All patients in whom a treatment decision has been made under Table 1 should perform home blood pressure monitoring using a validated upper-arm device. Patients should take two readings one minute apart in the morning before medications and two readings one minute apart in the evening, on at least three and preferably seven consecutive days, and transmit their readings to the care team weekly through the patient portal, secure messaging, or telephone. The care team reviews the weekly average systolic and diastolic readings.
recommendations.scope_notes: Applies to patients in whom a treatment decision has been made under Table 1.

recommendations.title: Home Blood Pressure Office Equivalence
recommendations.content: A home average of 135/85 millimeters of mercury (mmHg) or higher is considered equivalent to an office reading of 140/90 millimeters of mercury (mmHg).
recommendations.scope_notes: The source does not explicitly define paired-component comparison semantics for the blood pressure thresholds.

source_location.source_text: A home average of 135/85 mmHg or higher is considered equivalent to an office reading of 140/90 mmHg.

recommendations.title: Notify Clinician of Elevated Home Averages
recommendations.content: The responsible clinician should be notified when the weekly home average is 135/85 millimeters of mercury (mmHg) or higher, or exceeds a lower threshold set by the clinician for patients with diabetes or chronic kidney disease; this is a routine notification unless readings indicate a hypertensive crisis.
recommendations.scope_notes: The lower threshold for patients with diabetes or chronic kidney disease is clinician-set; no numeric lower threshold or complete hypertensive crisis classification is supplied.

source_location.source_text: The responsible clinician should be notified when the weekly home average is 135/85 mmHg or higher, or exceeds a lower threshold set by the clinician for patients with diabetes or chronic kidney disease

recommendations.title: Repeat Severe Home Readings and Contact Clinic
recommendations.content: Any single reading above 180/120 millimeters of mercury (mmHg) should be repeated after five minutes; if it remains above 180/120 millimeters of mercury (mmHg) the patient should contact the clinic the same day.
recommendations.scope_notes: The source does not define paired-component comparison semantics or further emergency management.

recommendations.title: Missing Readings Reminders and Barrier Assessment
recommendations.content: If a week passes without readings, a reminder should be sent to the patient. After three reminder attempts on different days without readings, the care team should contact the patient directly to identify barriers to monitoring.

recommendations.title: Home Readings Review after Medication Start or Change and with Lifestyle Modification Alone
recommendations.content: For patients starting or changing medication, the seven-day home average should be reviewed two to four weeks after the change, in addition to the laboratory follow-up in Table 2. Patients managed with lifestyle modification alone should have their home readings reviewed at the follow-up visit scheduled under Table 1.
